report:
Conclusion: The claim is not supported by the best current evidence. Early case-control studies produced mixed results, but they were vulnerable to recall/reporting bias because women with breast cancer may disclose past abortions differently than healthy controls. More rigorous prospective cohort studies and reviews by major cancer and OB-GYN bodies have found no causal increase in breast cancer risk after induced abortion. The National Cancer Institute states that ACOG’s 2009 committee concluded “more rigorous recent studies demonstrate no causal relationship,” and expert panels convened by NCI and ACOG reached the same conclusion. The American Cancer Society and Susan G. Komen similarly summarize that abortion is not related to increased breast cancer risk. A 2018 updated meta-analysis also notes that prospective evidence did not support a positive association. Some advocacy-linked meta-analyses claim an association, but they rely heavily on older retrospective designs and are not the consensus position.

Bottom line: Having an abortion should not be considered a proven breast cancer risk factor based on current mainstream scientific evidence.
